why: Chapters are read in a fixed order and unused time is lost, so the only sensible policy is greedy: each evening, read chapters while the next one still fits. A single pointer into chapters walks forward while you loop over evenings.
hints: Is there ever a reason to read fewer chapters than fit on an evening? Leftover minutes are discarded anyway.
Walk through evenings with a pointer i at the next unread chapter; while chapter[i] fits in the remaining minutes, read it and subtract.
Return the 1-based evening on which the last chapter is finished. O(len(chapter) + len(evening)).
pitfalls: A chapter that does not fit blocks the evening entirely; you cannot skip ahead to a shorter later chapter.
Leftover minutes do not carry over to the next evening.
If the evenings run out before the book is finished, return -1.
statement:
A book has chapters that must be read in order. chapter[i] is the number of minutes chapter i takes, and evening[j] is the number of minutes you have on evening j (evenings are numbered from 1).

Each evening you read as many consecutive unread chapters as fit in that evening's minutes. A chapter is started only if it can be finished the same evening, so chapters are never split. Unused minutes are lost; they do not carry over.

Return the number (1-based) of the evening on which you finish the last chapter, or -1 if the evenings run out first.

Example: chapter = [3,2,1], evening = [2,5,3,3]

  • Evening 1 (2 minutes): chapter 0 needs 3, does not fit. Nothing read.
  • Evening 2 (5 minutes): chapter 0 (3) fits, 2 left; chapter 1 (2) fits, 0 left.
  • Evening 3 (3 minutes): chapter 2 (1) fits. The book is finished.

The answer is 3.
constraints:
• 1 <= chapter.length, evening.length <= 10^5 (not stated in the source)
  • 1 <= chapter[i], evening[j] <= 10^9 (not stated in the source)
